newsitem.title: FRANCE: MEPs approve EU reaction to U.S. anti-Cuba law.
newsitem.headline: MEPs approve EU reaction to U.S. anti-Cuba law.

text.p: A planned European Union defence against U.S. anti-Cuba trade laws won approval on Friday from the European Parliament, which agreed to examine the proposal in record time so that it could take effect swiftly.
But the proposal may have to be re-submitted for approval by MEPs if EU foreign affairs ministers decide on October 28 to change its legal base, rapporteur Peter Kittlemann told Reuters.
Denmark has said it will block the EU's so-called anti-boycott regulation unless there is a change in the legal base.
Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said on Wednesday that Copenhagen could not accept the use of article 235 of the EU treaty.
Article 235 allows the EU to act in policy areas not specified elsewhere in the treaty and is seen with suspicion by governments wary of ceding too much authority to Brussels.
One option said to be under consideration is to base the legislation on article 113 (EU trade policy).
"We are convinced the legal base should be 235," Kittlemann said. "In the (EP) debate today, no-one agreed with the Danish position."

The MEP said he thought Denmark would voice its reticence next Monday but not demand a change. However, if Council did opt to alter the proposal -- COM(96)420 -- it would first have to consult Parliament, he said.
MEPs asked for three amendments to the Commission's text, including a change in the makeup of the committee which will be set up to help the Commission administer the legislation.
MEPs said the representatives of the member states sitting on the committee should have a purely advisory role.
This was to prevent member states tying the Commission's hands and slowing down implementation of the anti-boycott measures, Kittlemann said.

Diplomats say the other 14 EU member states have accepted the use of article 235 as the legal base for action but Denmark has been made especially sensitive to issues of sovereignty by a pending court case on the issue.

A group of citizens have filed a suit saying that Denmark's signature of the Maastricht treaty contravenes the national constitution by transferring too much political and judicial authority to supranational EU institutions.
